speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The Ministry of Manpower (MOM) has assessed that there is no conflict of interest for Members holding Singtel shares to participate in this debate and to vote on the Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: In the interest of transparency, I declare that I am a holder of Singtel Special Discounted Shares (Singtel SDS) as a Central Provident Fund (CPF) member.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The CPF is a key pillar of Singapore's social security system and has been updated over the years to meet our members' changing needs and ensure its continued effectiveness.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: It updates a legacy arrangement by enabling the transfer of Singtel SDS from the CPF Board to the Central Depository (CDP) accounts of SDS holders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This will benefit SDS holders by enabling them to manage their shares directly.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The SDS scheme was introduced in 1993 to give Singaporeans a stake in Singapore's economic success through share ownership.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: During Singtel's initial public offering (IPO) that year, where 11% of its total shares were traded for the first time, CPF members were offered the opportunity to buy Singtel shares at a discounted price using their CPF savings, first in 1993 and again in 1996.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This was an option given to CPF members.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: And though it was not compulsory, many chose to take this up.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: At that time, many CPF members were unfamiliar with share ownership.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Hence, to support them, the CPF Board was appointed as the trustee to facilitate these purchases.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Since then, these Singtel SDS have been held in CDP accounts under CPF Board's trusteeship.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Today, Singaporeans are more financially savvy and familiar with share ownership.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Many have their own CDP accounts and are experienced in trading shares.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Over the years, the SDS scheme has benefited many CPF members, the youngest of whom are now above 50 years old.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: In 1993 and 1996, SDS holders were able to buy their Singtel SDS with an upfront discount.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Those who held on to their shares also received loyalty shares equal to 40% of their initial holdings, along with regular dividends.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This does not include the interest earned on those dividends.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: In fact, their total dividends received alone would have exceeded both the CPF savings used to purchase the Singtel SDS and the interest they would have otherwise received in their CPF Ordinary Account.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Following the Singtel Group's proposal to transfer the Singtel SDS from the CPF Board to SDS holders, MOM and the CPF Board consulted relevant agencies to assess the proposal's impact on SDS holders and whether this would be beneficial to CPF members.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The SDS scheme has already achieved its intent of building up assets of CPF members.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The legacy arrangement where the CPF Board is the trustee for members' SDS is no longer necessary, given that Singaporeans are more financially savvy and familiar with share ownership.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Amongst the current Singtel SDS holders, close to three in five now have their own individual CDP accounts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: With the transfer, SDS holders can hold and manage their shares directly.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: They will also benefit indirectly as the Singtel Group will have greater flexibility to carry out corporate actions in a timely manner for them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: We have worked and will continue to work with the relevant parties, including MAS and SGX, to ensure a smooth transfer.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This includes availing options to SDS holders to ensure that their interests are protected and allowing them the flexibility to decide how they would want to manage their Singtel SDS moving forward.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: For those who prefer to keep their Singtel SDS, no action is required.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: For the three in five who have their own individual CDP accounts, also known as direct accounts in the Bill, we will automatically transfer their Singtel SDS to their individual CDP accounts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This consolidates all Singtel shares of an SDS holder into one account, making it easier for the holder to monitor and manage their shares.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: For the remaining two in five who do not have CDP accounts, we will automatically transfer their Singtel SDS to designated CDP accounts under their respective names, also known as "designated shares account", in the Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: This account will be created specifically to only hold Singtel SDS and its related entitlements.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Singtel SDS in designated CDP accounts will remain under the SDS scheme, which means that these SDS holders will largely continue to receive similar treatment and support as they do today.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: They will continue to receive future dividends in their CPF Ordinary Accounts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: If they sell their Singtel SDS at any point of time in the future, they can opt to receive the sale proceeds either in their CPF Ordinary Accounts or in cash.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: For SDS holders who prefer not to retain their Singtel SDS, they may choose to sell and receive their sale proceeds either in their CPF Ordinary Account or in cash.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Those who wish to keep their proceeds in their CPF Ordinary Accounts to earn higher interest may continue to do so.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Those who do not wish to make a decision now will still have the option to sell at any one point in time in the future, including after the transfer exercise.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: We have worked with CPF Board and Singtel Group to reach out to all SDS holders regarding the proposed transfer.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: All SDS holders would have received a hard copy notification letter in April 2026, issued jointly by the CPF Board and Singtel Group.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: It informs them of their Singtel SDS holdings, the options available to them and where they can seek clarifications and assistance.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Dedicated touchpoints have been set up to assist SDS holders on enquiries and sales.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: These span multiple channels, including a dedicated hotline, website, SingPost branches and CPF service centres across Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: SDS holders who wish to sell can do so either online, in-person at SingPost branches or through select SGX brokers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: We will conduct targeted outreach to help them understand their options.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: We have also put in place safeguards to help protect all SDS holders from potential scams.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: Through these efforts, SDS holders will be able to make an informed decision as to which option best meets their needs, while ensuring that whichever option they choose – either to sell or to keep their shares – the process is kept simple and safe.

speaker: The Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash) (for the Minister for Manpower)
text: The objective of the SDS scheme has already been achieved.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This is real money that can help a worker's family and make retirement a bit more secure.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: That is why we must make this transition safe, simple and supportive.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: SDS was a simple but powerful idea: give Singaporeans a stake in our economy through share ownership.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In other words, it helped workers turn wages into wealth, step by step, over time.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Even as Singtel may stand to benefit from the scheme through an easing of its administrative requirements and the ease of undertaking future corporate actions to enhance its own shareholder value, ultimately, Singaporeans will benefit from such an exercise.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, the closure of the Singtel SDS scheme also presents a timely opportunity to reflect on its successes, its inconsistencies and the broader question of how we truly enable Singaporeans to have a tangible stake in our nation's wealth.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Before I proceed, I wish to declare that I am not old enough to obviously have SDS shares, but I do have regular Singtel shares.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To understand the unique and what appears to be a one-off Singtel SDS scheme, we must look back at what then-Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong stated as the goal of his Government – to make Singapore a share-owning society.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: A statement by Singtel on its website explains it best: that the SDS scheme is a legacy scheme introduced in 1993, as part of the Government's efforts to give Singaporeans a stake in Singapore's economic success through share ownership.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: On this note, the 1993 and 1996 SDS exercises were arguably ahead of its time in inclusive wealth creation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: By offering shares at a massive discount as low as $1.90 for the ST "A" shares in 1993, and $2.50 for the ST2 shares in 1996, the Government ensured that even the smallest retail investor was in the money from day one.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This was by design, and then-Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong stated the 45% generous discount was to encourage long-term share ownership.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For many Singaporeans, especially those approaching retirement, this kicker is a vital addition to their requirement adequacy.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is a departure from the standard CPF investment scheme, where sale proceeds must typically be returned to the CPF account.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While I am supportive of this arrangement, what is the Government's rationale for why the SDS proceeds are treated differently?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Furthermore, the amount withdrawn for SDS does not require the payment of accrued interest upon sale.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This highlights a glaring inconsistency in our system.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Why is it that when a Singaporean uses his or her CPF savings for a home, which the Government has called an appreciating asset and a store of value, they must pay back the principle plus accrued interest.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Yet, for a CPF Investment Scheme (CPFIS) investments, no such requirements exists.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Government's long-standing justification is that this safeguards retirement adequacy.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To quote from the frequently asked question (FAQ) section on the CPF Board's website, "refunding both the principal amount and accrued interest ensures your retirement savings are fully restored to what they would have been if they had remained in your CPF account.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Without this refund, your retirement funds would be permanently reduced." Yet, from a financial investment under the CPFIS, which is arguably more volatile and which the Government has itself noted in the past, underperforms the 2.5% Ordinary Account rate for many CPF members, no such accrued interest is clawed back.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Is the Government suggesting that housing is a value-destructive asset that will ultimately permanently reduce the value of one's retirement savings due to its leasehold nature, while financial investments are value appreciating and bear less risk of endangering our retirement funds?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I hope the Minister can clarify the policy logic behind the distinction.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Returning to former Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong's National Day Rally speech in 1992, I note that, in the addition to Singtel, a company was to be set up to run the electricity and gas departments of the PUB, which I believe is now corporatised as the SP Group, and remains wholly owned by Temasek Holdings today.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Emeritus State Minister Goh went on further to say that the Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) and the Port of Singapore Authority (PSA) will be corporatised and publicly listed.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Their shares will appreciate as long as Singapore continues to be stable and prosperous and good management is in charge of the companies.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Fast forward to today, SMRT was listed and then privatised by Temasek Holdings subsequently, but there was no SDS.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: PSA was never listed, and its real estate arm, Mapletree Investments, continue to be private as well.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In 1994, after the listing of Singtel, former President Mr Ong Teng Cheong even shared in his President's Address, "The Singapore Telecom flotation was a resounding success: 1.4 million citizens bought Group A shares.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Significantly, people are holding on to them as long term investments instead of selling them immediately for quick profit.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The next likely one will be the PUB electricity and gas departments in two to three years' time.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Government will use these privatisations to enhance the assets of Singaporeans." The automated creation of CDP accounts under section 26C is a commendable administrative move and could serve as a blueprint for future Government-led asset transfers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, I am concerned that the closure of the SDS scheme signals an end to the share-owning society vision.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As a Member of Parliament who was only in primary school back then, will the Minister enlighten me on what happened to all these bold and attractive plans to enhance the assets of Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Why was it that there was only one SDS scheme?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Does the Minister and the Government not see the value and enhancement to Singaporeans' retirement savings with the SDS scheme?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As I have shared in my past speeches, we can give this current generation of Singaporeans a stake in the country via a meaningful IPO of the next wave of various private companies held by Temasek and encourage them to list on the Singapore Stock Exchange to fulfil the promises set more than 30 years ago.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Government will also be leading by example as part of its suite of measures under the recently introduced Equities Market Development Programme.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: More importantly, the point here is not just about a one-off distribution of shares and a discount to Singaporeans whenever a company goes to an IPO.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Workers' Party has advocated in our manifesto for enabling Singaporeans to co-invest their CPF savings with GIC.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It is about giving citizens a stake in the long-term strategic growth of our sovereign wealth.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If you want to generate real net worth for Singaporeans and provide a legacy for their children, you must move beyond being property asset rich but cash poor.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I suggest the Government consider a Temasek or GIC for every Singaporean model.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This will not only provide a financial safety net but also foster a generation of financially literate citizens who understand the value of a long-term strategic investment and who have an interest and a stake in national policy.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Allow me to conclude in Mandarin, Mr Speaker.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, in 1993, Singtel was officially listed as a public company and the Government launched the SDS scheme, allowing citizens to share in the nation's economic gains through broad-based share ownership.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I was only six years old that year.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: More than 30 years on, at 39, I have only now come to truly appreciate the historical significance and importance of that scheme.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Had the Government fulfilled its promise to extend similar discounted share schemes to companies, such as PUB, SMRT and PSA, would our retirement security be considerably more robust today?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: What I wish to emphasise today, however, is that we cannot remain confined to a framework of waiting for the Government to occasionally distribute "one-off" discounted shares or vouchers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Workers' Party has advocated in our manifesto for enabling Singaporeans to co-invest their CPF savings with GIC.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is not a call for "handouts" or "red packets" from the Government – it is about giving citizens a stake in the long-term strategic growth of our sovereign wealth.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It is my sincere hope that the passage of this Bill does not mark the end of Singapore's vision of a share-owning society, but rather the beginning of a new chapter – one in which we seriously revisit how Singaporeans and the Government can invest together, participating fairly and directly in the nation's wealth creation, and achieving what it truly means to keep wealth among the people.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The Singtel SDS scheme, which we are wrapping up today, is one such example.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: There were others over the years in different forms, such as the New Singapore Shares, the Progress Package and Growth Dividends.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: More than a social distribution, they represent the sharing of the nation's success with our citizens, reminders that we all have a stake in the Singapore story.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: We face structural shifts in our society that are both inevitable and expensive: an ageing population, rising healthcare and social spending, massive investments required for climate resilience.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: This increases structural pressures mean we cannot rely on Budget surpluses to fund this kind of generous redistribution we saw in previous years.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Each generation, having contributed to this nation in turn, also deserves to partake in the fruits of their labour.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: I was actually asked this question: what are the Singtel SDS shares of our generation?

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: I leave this as a philosophical question for the House to ponder.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: On the operational aspects, I believe we are in good hands.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Instead of the how, I would like to touch on the why.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: This is a significant departure from how we have always approached the CPF, a system built on the tight discipline to ensure long-term retirement adequacy.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: For years, the fundamental covenant of the CPF system has been clear.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Funds utilised from CPF must be returned to the CPF.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: By allowing a direct cash-out today, we are departing from this long-standing principle.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: We have upheld CPF principles for decades for good reasons.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Are there sufficient reasons to depart from them now?

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The reason given that the scheme has met its original intent does not fully answer the question.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: We must remember these Singtel shares are originally purchased using CPF monies.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Proceeds will be returned to CPF accounts upon sale.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Nor can we rely on the reasoning of simplifying "direct ownership" under the CDP because even under the transfer plan, specially designated CDP accounts for those who do not already have one.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: These accounts are under the shareholders' names but restricted in function to only handle transactions and profits from SDS shares and proceeds from those special CDP accounts are automatically channelled back to CPF by default.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: So, clearly, a path to return funds from CDP to the CPF directly already exists.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: This is not about trying to meddle in what people do with their own money.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: It is about protecting the rules of the system that has served us well.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: By opening this door, will there be further calls for waivers and exceptions under other circumstances for cash-out?

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: This is also about protecting our most financially vulnerable senior citizens.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: I understand that SDS shareholders and now in their 50s and above.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: They are already eligible to withdraw a portion of CPF savings at age 55.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: For those who met their retirement funds, these proceeds are merely an additional bonus.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Even if this bonus ends up back into their CPF, they would still have been able to take this additional sum in cash anyway.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: I understand all these, but I have reservations for the shareholders who have not even met their basic retirement fund.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The media reported about 20,000 members with low CPF balances and no CDP accounts.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: For them, these shares are not simply a "bonus".

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: They may form an important part of their retirement adequacy.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Would it not be safer for sale proceeds to return to CPF by default as has always been the practice.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: This would continue protecting retirement adequacy for members who have already met their retirement needs could still choose to withdraw their monies in cash.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Different households will have different realities and priorities.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: I also appreciate that some members may prefer to retain flexibility through their Ordinary Account, particularly for housing, healthcare, education or other long-term financial needs.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: But I strongly encourage those members who have not yet met their Basic Retirement Sum, if their circumstances allow, to consider transferring part or all of their proceeds back into their CPF.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: I would also like to offer a tip for those who decide to do so.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: For those who have not met the Basic Retirement Sum, please check your eligibility for the Matched Savings Retirement Scheme (MRSS).

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Under MRSS, every dollar voluntarily topped up to $2,000 a year, will be matched dollar-for-dollar by the Government.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: So, for shareholders who do not urgently need to utilise all the proceeds immediately, this scheme can significantly stretch the long-term value of the SDS proceeds.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: This could translate to close to $13,600 in retirement savings over time.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Now that I have highlighted this possible option, this tip, I would encourage the CPF Board to also help communicate this clearly to eligible members so that they can make informed decision based on their financial circumstances and priorities.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Let us do better for our most vulnerable seniors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I am the chief economist emeritus of a wealth management and advisory firm.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, unlike the Minister of State, I do not unfortunately hold any shares in Singtel SDS or otherwise although I regret that that does not necessarily make me all that much younger than him.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Unlike the declarations of the other Members in this House, they have gleefully declared that they are too young to receive SDS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Returning agency to Singaporeans is always welcome and even just on the spaces alone, the Bill will have my support.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Still, I have three points that I wish to make which relate to the treatment of stocks for deceased shareholders, whether the Bill may inadvertently open up less sophisticated Singaporeans to scam risk, and most generally, why the Government appears to have retreated on schemes that can expand share ownership of state-linked firms?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: First, I believe that that many of us have in our Meet-the-People Sessions encountered cases where the relative of the deceased resident has sought to sell their loved one's Singtel's SDS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Doing so required a special appeal to CPF, an extended and involved process just to recover what was often a relatively small amount of money.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Would the process be even more inaccessible now after the transfer to individual CDP accounts?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My understanding is that the CDP account of a deceased person may be accessed by a legally appointed personal representative of the estate, such as the executor of the will or the administrator in the event that there is no will.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But obtaining grants or probates or letters of administration are typically costly matters, especially for estates valued at more than $50,000.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even for smaller estates, the Public Trustee can assist with administration, but there are nevertheless costs involved.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This cost could sit easily outweigh the value of the residual Singtel SDS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After the passage of the Bill, will the Government have a low-cost mechanism to accommodate such eventualities, other than relying on the Public Trustee for smaller estates?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Otherwise, we may be left with a situation where Singtel shares are held in CDP accounts in the deceased name with no effective means of transfer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Alternatively, we may wish for CPF to remain a trustee in such special circumstances and perform the share disposal at the market price before transferring proceeds to the deceased's consolidated CPF balances.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Relatedly, is there a possibility that thousands of these CPF accounts might become zombie accounts should related family members be unaware that their departed relatives actually hold such shares?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Will the CPF nomination originally made by members continue to apply after the shares are transferred to CDP?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If not, what mechanism is there to ensure that the Public Trustee's Office can identify and contact potential beneficiaries?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Separate from deceased account holders, I should also point out that the complexity of the transfer mechanism sketched out in the new sections 26C and D may impose a non-trivial, ongoing administrative burden.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I appreciate that this complexity may be necessary to preserve the veracity of shareholders.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Still, perhaps, the Minister of State could share with us an estimate of how many such account transfers would need to be affected in future and if the Civil Service has already transmitted a set of standardised operating procedures to security firms to guide them on practical implementation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Taken together, there is now a clear route to encash these discounted stocks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Alas, the increased flexibility of allowing the withdrawal of equity sales proceeds were well meaning, also means that there could be a double-edged sword with unscrupulous fraudsters and scammers, potentially already licking the teeth at the prospect of accessing this pool of previously locked up funds.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is exacerbated by how most of the original discounted shareholders are now seniors who may be unsophisticated in the operation of stock trading accounts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I am unable to conjure up all the possible scenarios for such nefarious actions, but it behooves me to ask how the Government will pursue its duty of care to ensure that this unlocking of wealth does not go awry owing to financial illiteracy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What measures will CPF and Singtel take to educate their shareholders on the possible risks of scams during this transition period and will there be a dedicated hotline or other channels of assistance that can help this group navigate the CDP system safely?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: At the very least, we should ensure that basic safeguards aligned with the ones we already have in place for scams, such as cooling off periods, are adapted to this channel.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But since that first step, there have been no further efforts to offer discounted shares to the public.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is despite how several Government-linked corporations (GLCs) have been listed since – ST Engineering in 1997, SingPost and SMRT in 2000, and Semcorp in 2002, among others.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Despite these further opportunities for more stock ownership by ordinary Singaporeans, the Government had demurred.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If anything appears to have gone in the other direction, favouring either privatisation under the rubric of Temasek, or choosing property trust as a listing platform.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The reason cannot simply be because we have already accomplished the goal of making Singapore a shareholding society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In one fell swoop then, the Government had raised the share ownership rate from less than 9% to more than half, which is similar to the rate today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, if the goal was to raise the prevalence of share ownership among Singaporeans, this was already achieved in 1993.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The decision to further issue discounted Singtel shares must surely then have been motivated by other goals listed by then Finance Minister Richard Hu – to give Singaporeans an opportunity to share in the upside of the country's success and to imbue in them a stronger stake in the country.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If so, then the absence of more discounted share offerings tied to the listings of other GLCs since strike me as missed opportunities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One could alternatively argue that Singaporeans all enjoy indirect exposure to stocks via our sovereign wealth funds – GIC and Temasek.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This may be so, but given how these funds operate with little or no direct input from the average Singaporean, it is difficult to see how this very indirect ownership via these funds foster a sense that they have any direct stake in the country's success.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I believe that more legislation specific to the Lifetime Retirement Investment Scheme is to follow, and there is a fair degree of excitement over how a more explicit involvement of CPF account holders in the local stock market might further revive the SGX's fortunes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I trust that the amendments here, which appear to set the stage for proceeds and benefits that may accrue to any such Lifetime Retirement Investment Scheme to be credited back to the members' account, does not preclude a more consequential debate on the details of this scheme within this House when the time comes.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: It was a bold initiative, introduced in 1993, that enabled ordinary Singaporeans to participate in nation-building and share in the growth of Singapore's flagship telecommunications provider.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Back in 1993, the scheme was conceptualised with the CPF Board appointed as the trustee, to facilitate Singaporeans' share purchases, as many then were unfamiliar with owning shares.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Today, more than 30 years on, the context has changed significantly.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Singaporeans are more financially literate, markets are more accessible and the administrative structures that once made sense may no longer be necessary.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: However, from a consumer protection standpoint, this Bill is not just a technical amendment.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: It is a significant shift in responsibility: from the system to the individual.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Previously, these shares were held within a CPF-linked framework.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: There were built-in safeguards, including restrictions on withdrawals and a trustee structure that provided a degree of discipline.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: With this Bill, these safeguards are effectively removed.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This creates exposure to new risks, which we must mitigate.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Allow me to highlight three key concerns from the perspective of consumers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Some may have held these shares passively for decades.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: For them, this change may be perceived simply as an opportunity to "unlock cash".

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Second, the issue of financial literacy and decision-making.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Owning shares directly in the market requires a certain level of understanding – of price volatility, timing and transaction processes and costs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In our experience at CASE, when consumers are placed in unfamiliar financial situations, they can be vulnerable and may inadvertently make sub-optimal decisions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Once these shares are directly owned and easily tradable, they become a potential target.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Many in this House would be familiar with salespeople who approach Singaporeans unsolicited, asking consumers to purchase a course or a product using the latest Government grants.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: What is there to stop bad actors who seek to persuade or pressure individuals to tap on the SDS transfers to convince these shareholders to sell their shares and channel the proceeds into unsuitable or even fraudulent investments.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Bad actors could also convince unsuspecting consumers in downloading a fake trading application, and scam victims.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We have seen similar patterns whenever consumers gain access to newly liquid assets.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But they do call for a stronger consumer protection framework to accompany its implementation.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Communications should be clear, simple and tailored to different groups, especially our seniors.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Consumers must understand that once they sell these shares, the proceeds are no longer protected within CPF and decisions taken are not easily reversed.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Second, the introduction of light-touch safeguards at the point of sale.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This is not about restricting choice but about encouraging informed decision-making.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We urge the relevant agencies to closely monitor the situation during the transition period.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: There should also be strong and visible public messaging to warn consumers against unsolicited advice or high-pressure sales tactics.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In addition, financial advisers should be required to exercise heightened care when recommending the liquidation of these shares, particularly for vulnerable clients.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Fourth, support for consumers who may need assistance.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Not all Singaporeans are comfortable navigating CDP accounts or trading platforms.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Accessible help channels, including hotlines and physical touchpoints, will be important to ensure that no one is left behind.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This should examine outcomes, such as how many consumers liquidate their shares, whether there are concerning patterns among vulnerable groups and whether complaints relating to scams or misselling increase in tandem.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Such a review would allow us to respond quickly and timely if unintended consequences arise.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But with greater autonomy must come stronger support and safeguards, especially for those who may be less equipped to navigate these decisions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: At CASE, we strongly believe that consumer empowerment must go hand-in-hand with consumer protection.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: If we get this balance right, we can ensure that this transition will benefit all Singaporeans and not just the financially savvy, but also the more vulnerable among us.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For many, the value of these shares has increased several-fold over time, even before accounting for dividends and loyalty shares.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This was not just a financial scheme; it reflected a broader principle – that Singaporeans should have a stake in Singapore's success.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, I would like to ask, first, why have we not seen much more initiatives since then?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And as we invest in new growth areas, such as AI, digital infrastructure and emerging sectors, will there be opportunities for Singaporeans to participate in these national growth engines?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It simplifies the structure and gives members direct control over their assets.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: First, what triggered the need for this transfer at this point in time?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Were there specific limitations or inefficiencies in the previous trustee arrangement?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For those without CDP accounts, how many SDS holders fall into this group?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What will be the practical experience for them under the designated accounts?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Following the outbreak of the conflict in the Middle East, the increase in prices and in overall uncertainty exacerbating my concern over the retirement adequacy of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What is the policy rationale for this, especially for members below age 55?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In today's uncertain global environment, this could have implications for retirement adequacy, which remains an important concern.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: More importantly, does this risk sending an unintended signal for holders to sell rather than hold?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Since the First Reading of this Bill, the news headlines have been dominated by articles analysing whether individual SDS holders should sell or keep hold of their shares.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Should we be concerned with the market signals that are being sent out by this present Bill?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What discussions has the Government held with Singtel in that regard?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Allow me to speak briefly in Malay. :   Mr Speaker, a large proportion of SDS shareholders are seniors.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For them, these changes may be hard to understand.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must ensure that no one is left behind.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Information must be clear, easy to understand and delivered through appropriate channels – including face-to-face outreach.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What matters most is that every citizen is able to make a confident and informed decision. : Fifth, Sir, practical implementation points.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There may be individuals who do not respond to letters or may not even realise they still hold these shares.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Could the Minister share how many SDS holders have not engaged with outreach efforts so far and what additional measures are being taken to reach those who may be unaware of their holdings?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Additional touchpoints, such as Singpass notifications or CPF statements, may help ensure no one is left out.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Could the Minister elaborate on how the Government is ensuring that key concepts are truly understood, beyond translation into different languages?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Has the Government assessed whether this leads to optimal outcomes or whether some form of guidance or simple decision frameworks could help members make some informed choices?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If they choose not to act now, can they still do so next year or later without losing flexibility?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And after the transfer, will they continue to have full flexibility to hold or sell their shares at any time?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Clarity on this will be important as many members may prefer to take time before making a decision.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What safeguards are in place to protect, in particular, seniors from scams or financial exploitation during this transition?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Could the Minister share how many SDS holders have sold their shares since the announcement and how many have withdrawn proceeds in cash versus retaining them within CPF?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This will help us better assess behavioural outcomes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When designing policies, we must ensure that they do not result in windfall gains for a narrow group while the majority do not benefit.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Singapore's approach has been, use market mechanisms for efficiency while ensuring broad-based participation and inclusion.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This balance is critical not just for economic outcomes, but for maintaining trust and fairness in our system.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It modernises a legacy scheme and gives members greater control over their assets.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But its success will depend on clear communication, strong safeguards and ensuring that all Singaporeans, especially those less familiar with such matters, are able to benefit.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: More importantly, it prompts us to think about how future policies can continue to enable Singaporeans to share meaningfully in our nation's growth.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: It is also the birthday of one of my daughters, so I am doubly incentivised to make this a short speech.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: The Government's approach to sunset this programme is fair and it is prudent.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: It should save the CPF Board some resources.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: I hope that the Ministry can share an evaluation of the programme, both where it went well and areas for improvement.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: For example, did the scheme achieve its original objectives?

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Have we become more of a nation of investors?

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: In terms of the implementation approach, I support the Government's effort to reach out to legacy shareholders, many of whom are seniors, who are not financially savvy and who are more vulnerable to scams.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: For such seniors, trusted physical touchpoints that provide financial advice are crucial.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Can the Government clarify how long any physical touchpoints will be operating for?

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: I suggest that the CPF Board can provide resources to some of our community centres to set up physical touchpoints, especially those in neighbourhoods with a lot of seniors, such as those in Jalan Besar Group Representation Constituency (GRC).

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Can the Government confirm that Silver Generation ambassadors will also be empowered to direct our seniors to channels to receive appropriate financial advice?

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: I believe there is definitely demand for such advice.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Even I myself have been approached many times by my residents on what to do with their shares.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: When they ask me, I will reply: I am only a grassroots advisor, not your financial advisor.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: First, the spread of policy reviews on the CPF system this year reflects good policy housekeeping.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: It is a bit like taking care of a 70-year-old tree, since the CPF Board just celebrated 70 years last year.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: We need to keep pruning our policies – remove the unnecessary ones so that new ones with green shoots will flourish and provide more shade for all in retirement.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: One such policy with green shoots is the CPF Lifetime Retirement Investment Scheme.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: The scheme will empower Singaporeans to take a larger role in investing for their retirement.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: With the upcoming LRIS, other schemes which have outlived their purpose should be sunset, like the Singtel SDS.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: To the CPF member, there is no functional or financial difference between the two.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Hence, doing so could simplify the CPF system significantly.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Second, we should continue the spirit of the SDS programme – the spirit of providing ordinary Singaporeans access to the returns from otherwise privileged financial instruments.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: The spirit of sharing economic success directly with our citizens, who form the backbone and lifeblood of that very economic success.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: We have done this in a few ways.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Singapore has historically not shied from innovative policies that marry economic objectives with our social compact.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Singapore's land increases in value when our economy grows and because Singapore is a nation of property owners, many Singaporeans benefit from this land appreciation through owning HDB flats.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Such as the Growth Dividends of 2006 and 2008.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: But these surplus sharing programmes have been ad hoc for now.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Perhaps we can think of a longer-term programme to allow Singaporeans to have a stake in the economic upside of Singapore, even if they are no longer in the workforce and are not business owners.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Third, we should emulate the attitude of the Government in the 1990s.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: It was a Government that was not afraid of taking some policy risk.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Today, the SDS programme is seen positively because Singtel has done well; well, at least, Singtel shares have done well.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: But this was not a foregone conclusion when the scheme started.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: The company could have done poorly or the business environment could have been worse.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Yet the decision makers of that day decided that it was worth the policy risk.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Singaporeans, with their eyes wide open, took a bet with them.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: I hope this will continue in our Government schemes today.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: Minister Chee Hong Tat mentioned this in the previous debate for the previous Bill, to be able to take some policy risk.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: The Lifetime Retirement Investment Scheme, for example, is also not without policy risk.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: And I am glad that we are taking this bet together again.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: It was a good chapter in our nation-building story, with a happy ending.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: I support the closing of this chapter and look forward to CPF Board writing similar chapters in the future.

speaker: Mr Shawn Loh (Jalan Besar)
text: And may they all have happy endings too.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: I also note that two Members, particularly my friends from the Opposition, highlighted my relatively young age in a tongue-in-cheek manner, or rather, my experience, as I would like to see as.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: And I assure you that I would not use your lack of experience nor youth against you.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat, Ms Gho Sze Kee, Mr Patrick Tay and Mr Shawn Loh asked whether there would be similar opportunities for younger cohorts.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: In the 1990s, we took the decision to privatise the telecommunications portion of the Telecommunication Authority of Singapore into what is known as Singtel today.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: Singtel’s subsequent IPO in 1993 allowed the Government to offer Singaporeans an entry point into share ownership and to give them a stake in the nation’s growth.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: By these measures, the scheme had achieved its intended objectives.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: Since then, Singaporeans have become a lot more familiar with shareholding.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: Today, three in five SDS holders have CDP accounts.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: There is therefore less need for a scheme similar to SDS to serve as an entry point to share ownership.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: I want to highlight that beyond Singtel, there are other companies such as ST Engineering and SingPost that were also eventually listed on the Singapore Exchange and were subsequently owned by many Singaporeans among us.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: The Government has continued to use a range of measures to allow Singaporeans to share in the benefits of our progress, such as the SG Bonus cash payout in 2018 and SG60 Vouchers last year.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: Our CPF and housing policies have also enabled Singaporeans to build up assets over time.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: Mr Saktiandi asked about the rationale for the transfer of the Singtel SDS to the CDP.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: CPF Board operates with members’ best interests at heart and a strong duty of care.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: It is having assessed that it would benefit SDS holders that the Government decided to embark on this exercise.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: The upcoming transfer will benefit SDS holders by giving them greater flexibility to consolidate their shareholdings in their CDP accounts.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: They also have the option to sell and encash their SDS holdings anytime, if they wish.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: The transfer will also give Singtel Group the flexibility to carry out corporate actions in a timely manner.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: Under the trustee arrangement currently, communication for Singtel’s corporate actions to SDS holders are made through CPF Board.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: For example, during the scrip dividend exercise in 2020, notification letters to SDS holders were sent by CPF Board and time was required for CPF Board’s system to be changed to allow for the scrip crediting to take place.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: After the transfer, Singtel will be able to communicate with shareholders directly and execute corporate actions, such as scrip dividends, in a more timely and cost-efficient manner.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: SDS holders will also stand to benefit as they will be able manage their shares seamlessly.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: So, indeed, as Mr Saktiandi and Mr Loh mentioned, this Bill reflects good policy housekeeping by modernising a legacy arrangement.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: As demonstrated by this exercise, CPF Board regularly reviews and finds ways to update and streamline existing schemes and processes.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: Mr Saktiandi, Ms Gho and Mr Melvin Yong also asked about the reason for allowing the SDS proceeds to be withdrawn in cash without having to meet the CPF withdrawal rules and if this sends out a signal to sell rather than to hold the Singtel SDS.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: Mr Yong also spoke about the need for sufficient financial literacy.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: When the scheme was inaugurated, CPF members had a choice to be part of the Singtel SDS.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: Similarly, whether SDS holders should sell or keep their Singel SDS is a private decision that members must take, just as they did when they came onboard the scheme in 1993 and 1996.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: If they prefer liquidity, they can choose to sell.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: If they prefer to stay invested and to reap future gains, they can do so.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: We decided that the SDS sale proceeds would not be subject to the CPF withdrawal rules given that the SDS scheme has met its intent of enhancing the assets of CPF members.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: This arrangement also gives SDS holders options, and ensures that those who do not have individual CDP accounts are not disadvantaged; in fact, they can receive their sale proceeds in cash without even needing to open one.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: As mentioned, those who prefer to keep their sale proceeds in their CPF Ordinary Accounts to earn higher interest can still continue do so.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: We also welcome Ms Gho’s tip to encourage eligible SDS holders to top up their CPF Retirement Account under MRSS to receive a dollar-for-dollar matching grant from the Government.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: It is a safe and legal hack, and I would encourage you to let your residents know about it too.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: Around nine in 10 chose to receive the proceeds in cash.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: SDS holders have the flexibility to decide when they would like to sell.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: As mentioned in my earlier speech, even after the transfer, those who sell their SDS held in designated CDP accounts will still be able to withdraw the proceeds in cash without being subject to CPF withdrawal rules.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: We agree with the spirit of Members’ comments, that there are needs to be safeguarded as we update this legacy arrangement, so as not to disadvantage those who are less financially savvy.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: With this transfer, we have sought to ensure that every SDS holder has access to resources that support them in making an informed decision about how best to manage their Singtel SDS.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: For investors who already have individual CDP accounts, they will be able to consolidate shareholdings and manage them within the CDP framework that they are already very familiar with.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: For the SDS holders who do not have individual CDP accounts and who may be less familiar with investing, their shares will be transferred to designated CDP accounts.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: This means that these SDS holders will largely continue to receive similar treatment and support as today, even after their Singtel SDS is transferred to their designated CDP accounts.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: Specifically, on the sale process post-transfer, it will largely remain the same as today.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: On Mr Fadli Fawzi's question about charges, the sales process and charges during the period are the same as what they were prior to the exercise.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: To Mr Fadli's point on why we chose to create designated CDP accounts, this is in recognition that not everyone needs an individual CDP account, especially some of the SDS holders who do not intend to trade or hold other shares.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: The Government also cannot open individual CDP accounts on SDS holders' behalf.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: Doing so requires the members to complete comprehensive compliance screenings, including tax residency declarations and risk appetite assessments to ensure adherence to regulatory requirements and international tax obligations are fulfilled.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: SDS holders without an individual CDP account can apply to open one if they wish to trade actively or transact in other products.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: Mr Saktiandi, Mr Loh, Mr Fadli and Mr Yong raised important questions about the special outreach efforts undertaken to ensure that SDS holders who require greater assistance are not neglected.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: This is also an issue that is close to my heart.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: To support different segments of SDS holders, we have a range of measures in place.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: For SDS holders who are less comfortable with digital platforms, there are accessible, physical touchpoints.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: Staffing at these centres have been beefed up in anticipation of the higher load from walk-in queries.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: A dedicated hotline, 1713, has been set up for those who prefer to seek help over the phone.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: Information about the exercise is also available in print and via broadcast media, ensuring that it reaches those who may not have easy digital access.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: Key publicity collaterals and notification letters to SDS holders have also been translated into vernacular languages, ensuring that those who are more comfortable in their mother tongue can access important information clearly and easily.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: Some SDS holders may face physical accessibility challenges.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: CPF Board and Singtel are partnering the Agency for Integrated Care (AIC) to conduct door-to-door outreach and visits to nursing homes and care facilities.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: This ensures that even those who are homebound or residing in institutional care settings are personally reached and made aware of their options and the channels for assistance.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: Caregivers and family members assisting SDS holders are also welcome to engage any of the service touchpoints on their behalf.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: For those who have individual CDP accounts, their Singtel SDS will be treated as any other CDP shares and will form part of their estate.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: I would also like to highlight Assoc Prof Jamus Lim's point on administrative complexity.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: I want to just highlight that this is really a one-off exercise and the number of SDS to be transferred will be dependent on how many SDS holders who have decided to sell prior to the cut-off point that we have in November.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: And hence, the complexity is something that we have to balance and ensure that we are reasonable and prudent, and to accept some degree of administrative complexity in the short run, at least.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: We would like to emphasise that no action is required for those who wish to retain their Singtel SDS.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: SDS holders who are uncertain or need assistance can approach the readily available service touchpoints that I have mentioned earlier.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: Mr Saktiandi, Mr Yong, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim and Mr Tay have also raised concerns about the risk of scams during this exercise period.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: This is a legitimate and important concern today.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: We have built in multiple layers of safeguards into this exercise to protect SDS holders from potential scams.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: This ensures that individualised information is directed solely to the intended recipient.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: This ensures that sale proceeds can only flow to a pre-verified account and cannot be redirected to an unknown or unverified third-party account.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: We have also reiterated in our collaterals that CPF Board and Singtel will never ask or never request bank account details or any payment from SDS holders in connection with this exercise.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: The CPF Board and Singtel have incorporated clear scam advisories across all communications to SDS holders.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: SDS holders are reminded to remain vigilant and refer only to official communications and touchpoints.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: When unsure, SDS holders can always call the SDS hotline, 1713, or the 24-hour ScamShield anti-scam helpline for verification.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: We are closely monitoring the post-implementation situation and will respond quickly if any situation arises.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: I wanted to just add that the implementation thus far, has been smooth.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: The dedicated hotline and physical service touchpoints have been operating well, with queries being resolved promptly and efficiently.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: Perhaps due to the safeguards against scams, we have, thankfully, not received any complaints about residents being scammed thus far.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: Mr Loh also raised some other questions and suggestions about the CPF system.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: We note and thank him for his suggestions.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: Some Members have also called for more broad-based investment opportunities for CPF members to participate in.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: In fact, both Mr Loh and Mr Tay had mentioned the upcoming new investment scheme, which would also give Singaporeans another opportunity to benefit from investments schemes more broadly in a structured manner.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: We are developing the scheme further and will share details and updates in due course.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: There were several references to the discussion and policy thinking back in the day, when this particular scheme was raised, and I thought I should just flag up some of the comments that were highlighted by the then-Prime Minister Mr Goh Chok Tong on 9 March 1993, and I quote: "The Government's primary duty is to build the right conditions for Singaporeans to create wealth for themselves.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: These conditions include security, law and order, political stability, social discipline, a level-playing field, the free market, meritocracy and rewards in accordance with persons' abilities, both performance and contribution." Successive People's Action Party (PAP) Governments have done so.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: The Singtel SDS exercise is but one example.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: We have since moved into other programmes as well.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: There was a comment also made about whether was it because of the comments that were made in 1993 that we had a jump, in terms of our shareholding culture, in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: As such, the Singtel SDS had been a success, and successive PAP Governments have built on the success to where we are today.

speaker: Mr Dinesh Vasu Dash
text: This move reflects how far we have come since the scheme’s inception.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Are there any clarifications for Minister of State Dinesh?
